appraisal_events.evidence: En lisant son article du Figaro « en m'efforçant de me persuader qu'il était d'un autre », le narrateur passe du « sentiment de mon impuissance et de mon manque incurable de talent » à « autant de sentiment de ma force et d'espoir de talent » ; « Bah ! comment un lecteur peut-il s'apercevoir de cela ? » ; puis « je sentais bien que ce n'était pas vrai ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator raises himself by borrowing the eye of an anonymous admiring reader and the imagined support of ten thousand approvals, gaining real comfort and confidence; the narration simultaneously exposes the operation as a deliberate self-deception and closes by unmasking the worldly motive behind it, so the elevation is granted and undercut at once.

appraisal_events.evidence: Forcheville juge qu'« en épousant la veuve d'un juif il avait accompli le même acte de charité qu'un millionnaire qui ramasse une prostituée dans la rue », veut effacer « cet absurde nom de Swann » et « déclara qu'il l'adoptait » ; Mme de Guermantes, qui s'était « refusée à recevoir sa fille aussi bien que sa femme », dit : « si ça amuse le pauvre Swann de faire des bêtises et de ruiner son existence, c'est son affaire ».
appraisal_events.explanation: After his death Swann is posthumously downgraded by the social world: his name is treated as an absurdity to be erased by adoption, his marriage as something a nobleman charitably redeemed, and his life as a self-ruining folly. The narrator records this degradation while ridiculing its agents, notably Forcheville's family-bred genealogical vanity and the duchesse's comfortable detachment.

status_effects.explanation: Swann's local standing collapses posthumously: his name is stripped from his daughter, his marriage is reframed as a charity case, and the duchesse's refusal to receive his wife and daughter is restated as settled fact.

The same reversal that erases her father's name raises her sharply: she inherits an enormous fortune, becomes 'une des plus riches héritières de France', and is adopted into the noble name of Forcheville.
She now stands inside the Guermantes salon that had refused to receive Mlle Swann, and takes the initiative of having the duchesse present the narrator to her.

Though he wins the practical outcome, the narrator makes him ridiculous as the agent of the appraisal: his certainty that his name outranks La Rochefoucauld's comes from family gossip, and his self-image as a charitable rescuer is exposed as grotesque.
The reading is explicitly 'réconfortante' and converts his earlier suffering over the article into force and hope of talent, even though the passage marks the gain as borrowed and illusory.

ambiguities: The surface form « Mlle d'Éporcheville » is unstable in this very passage: the text reveals it as the narrator's double error (de l'Orgeville heard as d'Éporcheville, then Forcheville reconstituted as Éporcheville), so it names at once the different young woman of Saint-Loup's telegram and, mistakenly, Gilberte. The reference sheet carries « Mlle d'Éporcheville » both as a standalone entity and as an alias of Gilberte; the pre-recognition mentions are kept here under the standalone entry rather than merged into Gilberte.

The narrator's article-reading can be read either as a genuine, narrator-endorsed recovery of confidence ('lecture réconfortante', 'sentiment de ma force et d'espoir de talent') or as an exposed self-deception ('je me déchargeais sur les autres du devoir douloureux de me juger'; 'je sentais bien que ce n'était pas vrai'). It is annotated as a real but ironized elevation, since the passage grants the comfort and dismantles its grounds in the same movement.
